title: The Stalker

jokes.text: The show announcer's intro: 'and now, because the governor called... Larry Sanders!'
jokes.setup: Standard late-night announcer buildup to the host's entrance
jokes.punchline: 'because the governor called' — an absurd, unexplained non-reason delivered with complete straight-faced authority
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compact absurdist line. The non-sequitur reason for Larry's entrance — 'because the governor called' — is delivered with the gravitas of a real announcement, which makes it funnier. Pure economy of language. It's the kind of throwaway that a lesser show wouldn't bother with, but Larry Sanders rewards attention. Justifies the 7+ because it's the kind of gag only a smart writers' room produces.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank, you hang out with ed.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: Former sidekick Ed McMahon is suing the Star for calling him a drunk. Hank, you hang out with Ed. Could you clear this up for us?
jokes.setup: Larry frames the question as a serious request for clarification about Ed McMahon's sobriety
jokes.punchline: Hank solemnly confirms Ed is NOT a drunk — implying Hank has firsthand knowledge because they drink together, treating it as a credible denial
jokes.explanation: Works because Hank is precisely the kind of person who would validate a drunk's reputation while being oblivious to the implication. The audience laughter cue confirms the beat lands. Character-specific and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He is on crack. [Laughter] But, um... Kids... Just say no.

jokes.text: Larry asks Hank to vouch that Ed McMahon isn't a drunk; Hank solemnly says 'I know for a fact Ed is not a drunk.' Beat. 'He is on crack.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Hank, who 'hangs out with Ed,' to clear up the Star tabloid claim that McMahon is a drunk — playing on the implication Hank would know the truth
jokes.punchline: Hank solemnly confirms 'Ed is not a drunk' — then a beat — then 'He is on crack.' Followed by Larry's straight-faced 'Kids... just say no.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first genuinely great joke. The structure is immaculate: Larry sets up the denial as if it will exonerate McMahon, Hank delivers the exoneration with complete sincerity, then pivots to something far worse delivered with equal sincerity. The 'Kids... just say no' from Larry is the perfect button — mock-PSA gravity covering obvious discomfort. The joke requires both characters to play it dead straight for maximum effect, which is exactly what the show does. This is the Tambor/Shandling dynamic in miniature: Larry creates chaos, Hank makes it worse with absolute conviction. Justifies 8+ by comparable quality to the 'Snip snap' calibration anchor in terms of structure and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: without any renovation, it's being turned into a tgi friday's.

jokes.text: The Kennedys are selling their famous Palm Beach estate. Without any renovation, it's being turned into a TGI Friday's.
jokes.setup: Larry announces a newsworthy real estate story about the Kennedy estate
jokes.punchline: The venerable Kennedy property will become a TGI Friday's — the most aggressively banal chain restaurant imaginable — undercutting American royalty mythology
jokes.explanation: Solid late-night joke construction. The TGI Friday's specificity is key — it's not just 'a restaurant,' it's the exact brand of tacky Americana that most deflates the Kennedy mystique. Competent but not outstanding.

dialogue.line: the wet t-shirt contest will still be on tuesdays.

jokes.text: The wet t-shirt contest will still be on Tuesdays.
jokes.setup: Kennedy estate is becoming a TGI Friday's
jokes.punchline: The tacky Kennedy history (implied sexual scandals) is mapped onto TGI Friday's promotional events — the 'wet t-shirt contest' being both a TGI Friday's gag and a Kennedy family joke simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The tag works on two levels simultaneously — TGI Friday's sleaze + Kennedy family scandal lore — making it denser than a simple one-liner. The brevity and the double meaning give it good economy. The 'No more jokes, Larry' reaction from someone offscreen adds a layer of meta-commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No more jokes, Larry.

jokes.text: Michael Jackson has purchased a 12-foot albino snake. He named it — this is absolutely true — he named it Madonna.
jokes.setup: Celebrity news item about Michael Jackson buying a snake
jokes.punchline: The snake is named 'Madonna' — letting the audience supply the multiple layers of the joke (Jackson/Madonna rivalry, reptilian metaphor for Madonna, Jackson's eccentricity)
jokes.explanation: The 'this is absolutely true' qualifier is a classic late-night move — preempting the audience's disbelief to heighten the punchline. The joke trusts the audience to do the interpretive work. Competent late-night writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: he named it-- this is absolutely true. he named it Madonna.

jokes.text: Larry turns off the television mid-monologue and the scene cuts to his home at night.
jokes.setup: Larry has been doing a confident monologue about Michael Jackson naming a snake 'Madonna'
jokes.punchline: The abrupt cut from polished TV host to Larry alone, terrified, in his dark house — the juxtaposition of professional persona vs. private paranoid wreck
jokes.explanation: A structural/visual joke built into the editing. Larry turns off his own show mid-joke — the moment of transition from the performed Larry to the real one is the punchline. Smart show-craft that rewards attentive viewers. The comedy is in the contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: It's me. God, you scared the shit out of me.

jokes.text: Squirrel, my ass. It was something really big.
jokes.setup: Someone (Francine) suggests the roof noise was a squirrel
jokes.punchline: Larry's dismissal — 'Squirrel, my ass' — is delivered with total conviction, treating a potentially mundane noise as an existential threat
jokes.explanation: The line captures Larry's paranoid certainty perfectly. 'Squirrel, my ass' is punchy and character-specific — Larry is always one step past reasonable concern. The humor is in his complete conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It was one of those fucking tour buses. Maybe someone jumped off and ran onto the roof.

jokes.text: Your address is on all those maps. I know. How did you know that? When my sister was in town, she wanted to see where Tony Danza lives.
jokes.setup: Larry is worried that celebrity home maps expose him to stalkers
jokes.punchline: Francine casually reveals she used the very same maps — to find Tony Danza's house — undercutting any high-minded concern while also implying Tony Danza is the real draw
jokes.explanation: Two-layer joke: (1) the irony of Larry's girlfriend using the same maps he's worried about, and (2) the celebrity status joke — her sister wanted to see Tony Danza, not Larry. The Tony Danza specificity is perfect; it's a name that implies 'B-list adjacent' without being mean. Well-structured and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: When my sister was in town, she wanted to see where tony danza lives. Nice vacation.

jokes.text: Your sister's not in town, is she? [long pause]
jokes.setup: Francine has revealed her sister used the celebrity maps to find Tony Danza
jokes.punchline: Larry's question implies the roof noise and the map usage are connected — he's now suspicious of Francine's sister — followed by a telling pause where Francine apparently doesn't answer
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. The question is five words and it recontextualizes everything. The pause that follows (Francine apparently doesn't immediately deny it) is where the real joke lives. This is the Larry Sanders Show at its best — the comedy is in what isn't said.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Your sister's not in town, is she?

jokes.text: Have you been keeping mail from me — threatening letters? No. No more than usual. Wait a minute. What's the usual? You said not to tell you.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Beverly has been hiding threatening letters from him
jokes.punchline: Beverly confirms she has been hiding them — as per his own instructions — creating a perfect Catch-22 where Larry's desire for normalcy directly enables his danger
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed exchange. The 'no more than usual' is an instant classic line — Beverly's bureaucratic normalcy about celebrity death threats is perfectly calibrated. Then the Catch-22 of 'you said not to tell you' makes Larry the author of his own ignorance. This is sharp, character-specific comedy writing that perfectly captures the insular insanity of celebrity life. Justifies a high score.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No more than usual. Wait a minute. What's the usual?

jokes.text: The security brochure reads: 'John Lennon, Sharon Tate — these incidences could have been prevented by adequate security.' They're just preying on people's fears.
jokes.setup: Beverly hands Larry a Whitewood Security brochure
jokes.punchline: Larry reads the brochure's pitch — citing two of the most famous murder victims of the 20th century — and dismisses it as fear-mongering, which is both accurate and completely wrong given his actual situation
jokes.explanation: The comedy of denial: Larry correctly identifies the brochure as exploitative while being a genuine celebrity stalker target. The John Lennon/Sharon Tate specificity is dark and sharp. His dismissiveness is immediately ironic given what we know. Strong ironic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: John lennon, Sharon tate-- These incidences could have been prevented by adequate security

jokes.text: The Larry Sanders Look-alike contest. Alec Baldwin won, didn't he?
jokes.setup: Beverly mentions the Larry Sanders Look-alike contest winner will be on the show
jokes.punchline: Larry guesses 'Alec Baldwin won' — implying he thinks he looks like Alec Baldwin, or that Alec Baldwin entered a Larry Sanders look-alike contest, both of which are absurd ego-driven readings
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry vanity joke. The punchline works because it reveals Larry's self-image — he thinks he looks like Alec Baldwin. It's a precise, efficient character joke. High character integration score justified because only Larry could deliver this with straight-faced sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Alec Baldwin won, didn't he?

jokes.text: The look-alike winner reveals he always stays in Larry's same hotel room in Hawaii: '714 — the one with the bathtub?'
jokes.setup: The look-alike winner says he vacations where Larry vacations and stays where Larry stays
jokes.punchline: Larry enthusiastically confirms the specific room number, then asks about the bathtub — inadvertently validating the stalker behavior and providing more information
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed cringe escalation. Larry is so flattered by the attention that he fails to register the stalker red flags — even confirming his exact room number on live TV. The comedy is in the gap between what's happening (fan obsession) and how Larry processes it (flattery). Well-built.

dialogue.speaker: Look-alike
dialogue.line: I even stay in your favorite room. 714-- the one with the bathtub? Yeah. And the shower?

jokes.text: I promise, no guests will look like me. Sleep well.
jokes.setup: Larry wraps up the interview with the look-alike winner on-air
jokes.punchline: The sign-off 'Sleep well' is both a standard late-night closer and, given that he was just talking to what might be a stalker, a deeply ironic choice of words
jokes.explanation: The irony of 'sleep well' as a farewell after an implicit stalker encounter earns it a rewatch bonus. The joke only fully lands on retrospect — or for attentive viewers. Economy is high.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Good job.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Good job to you.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Good job, Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Good job yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Good job.

jokes.text: All I'm saying, Artie, is if it was a squirrel, it must have weighed 140 pounds and been able to walk erect.
jokes.setup: Artie apparently still thinks the roof noise was a squirrel
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'squirrel' description — 140 lbs, walking erect — is his paranoid logic taken to its logical absurd endpoint while being delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: The callback to the squirrel argument with the added specificity of '140 pounds and able to walk erect' is excellent. The comedy is in Larry's meticulous logical breakdown of why the squirrel theory is impossible — he's treating it like a criminal investigation. Very quotable, very Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You guys look like the two-captain-kirk episode from 'star trek.' Right, 'incident on rigel 7.'

jokes.text: I still say you should go with a 12-foot electrical fence. I think that's a little gaudy. Gaudy, hell — fry the motherfuckers.
jokes.setup: Larry expresses concern about security but objects to the aesthetic of an electrical fence
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Fry the motherfuckers' — delivered with total pragmatic calm — obliterates Larry's interior decorating objection with violent frontier logic
jokes.explanation: This is Artie in his purest form. Rip Torn's character is the show's id — he cuts through all pretense with blunt, profane, absolute logic. 'Gaudy, hell — fry the motherfuckers' is a perfect line: Larry's concern about aesthetics vs. Artie's concern about lethal efficacy. The juxtaposition of 'gaudy' and 'fry the motherfuckers' is inspired. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific. Justified high scores.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: 'Don't endanger the ship, spock. Kill us both.'

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're a gifted man.

jokes.text: You guys look like the two-Captain-Kirk episode from Star Trek. Right, 'Incident on Rigel 7.' 'Don't endanger the ship, Spock. Kill us both.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are both looking at the look-alike winner and Hank observes that Larry/his look-alike resemble the split-Kirk Star Trek episode
jokes.punchline: Artie not only knows the episode title but quotes it specifically — revealing an encyclopedic and incongruous Trek knowledge. The fake episode title and misquoted Spock line are absurdly confident
jokes.explanation: The joke has multiple layers: Hank's pop-culture analogy, Artie's improbable Trek knowledge, and the absurdly dramatic fake Spock quote. The confident delivery of wrong-sounding details ('Incident on Rigel 7' — the actual episode is 'The Enemy Within') adds an extra absurdist layer.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know, maybe one night I could do it on the ship. Not this--

jokes.text: Hey, what the fuck are you doing? He's sniffing my jacket, Artie. Just to see what cologne Larry wears.
jokes.setup: The look-alike winner is in the office after the taping
jokes.punchline: He is literally sniffing Larry's jacket — a perfect physical manifestation of obsessive fan behavior that is simultaneously horrifying and absurd
jokes.explanation: The jacket-sniffing is the episode's central visual gag and perfectly embodies the stalker theme. It escalates naturally from the hotel room conversation — this guy isn't just a fan, he's trying to physically inhabit Larry's identity. The matter-of-fact explanation ('just to see what cologne Larry wears') makes it more disturbing and more funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He's sniffing my jacket, Artie. Just to see what cologne Larry wears.

jokes.text: Larry's birthday is coming up on the 19th.
jokes.setup: The stalker is already sniffing Larry's jacket
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions Larry's exact birthday — information Larry hasn't shared with him — as if it's perfectly normal, deepening the horror-comedy
jokes.explanation: The escalation continues seamlessly. The birthday detail is delivered casually while Artie is still reacting to the jacket sniffing — the layering of creepy details builds perfectly. Economy is excellent — one line, massive implication.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The guy looked like linda hunt.

jokes.text: Artie physically wrestling the stalker; Hank trying to stop him — 'Easy, Artie! Sit down!'
jokes.setup: The stalker has been sniffing Hank's jacket and mentioning Larry's birthday; Artie intervenes physically
jokes.punchline: Artie — the veteran TV producer — is physically wrestling the man while Hank panics; the violence is wildly disproportionate to office protocol
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that works because of Artie — a Rip Torn physical confrontation is inherently funny because of who Rip Torn is. Character-specific: Artie doesn't call security, he handles it himself. The gap between 'TV producer in an office' and 'full physical struggle' is the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What I'd do if I was stalking somebody-- see where they live, then come back later to kill them.

jokes.text: The guy looked like Linda Hunt.
jokes.setup: Artie has apparently just physically removed the look-alike from the premises
jokes.punchline: Artie's only comment on the incident is a physical description — 'looked like Linda Hunt' — delivered as if this is the most important and relevant fact about the encounter
jokes.explanation: Five words, maximum comedy. The Linda Hunt comparison is perfectly chosen — an Oscar-winning actress known for playing characters much smaller/different than expected, with an immediately recognizable face. Artie reducing the entire stalker encounter to this one physical observation is peak Artie. The economy is near-perfect, and only Rip Torn's Artie could deliver this as the definitive end of the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: He stopped wearing a toupee because he realized in prison you don't need hair to be attractive.

jokes.text: What I'd do if I was stalking somebody — see where they live, then come back later to kill them.
jokes.setup: Larry explains why the stalker driving past his house after following him doesn't necessarily mean he's safe
jokes.punchline: Larry explains, from first principles, the tactical logic of celebrity stalking — 'come back later to kill them' — as if he's done the research
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny dark logic. Larry mapping out stalker strategy — 'see where they live, then come back later to kill them' — delivered as paranoid self-protection reasoning rather than self-awareness is chillingly funny. The line 'what I'd do if I was stalking somebody' is the setup, and the casual 'to kill them' is the dark punchline. Strong.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: I only have time to humor one neurotic obsession. Are we choosing this one? Next time, one of mine?

jokes.text: He stopped wearing a toupee because he realized in prison you don't need hair to be attractive.
jokes.setup: Larry and his companion discuss Mike Milken getting out of prison and stopping wearing a toupee
jokes.punchline: The implication that in prison, other qualities are more valued than hair — a dark joke about prison sexual dynamics delivered with total Larry nonchalance
jokes.explanation: A nicely dark prison joke with good economy. The toupee setup is unexpected (why would anyone discuss Milken's hair?) and the punchline about prison attractiveness works on dark implication. Solid.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: Yeah, or having living with one or having sex with one or a relationship or whatever we're doing here.

jokes.text: I only have time to humor one neurotic obsession. Are we choosing this one? Next time, one of mine?
jokes.setup: Francine is trying to decide whether to take Larry's stalker fears seriously
jokes.punchline: Her framing of Larry's fear as a 'neurotic obsession' to be managed in a quota — and the offer to trade obsessions — reveals the entire dynamic of their relationship
jokes.explanation: Sharp relationship comedy. The 'one neurotic obsession at a time' framing is both a great character line and a compact summary of why their relationship is complicated. The 'next time, one of mine' implies she has her own queued up — a perfect detail. Very efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, it's o.K. It's tom Hanks. He always jogs at this time. Tom!

jokes.text: These people think of you as a god, something beyond an ordinary human. That's one of the things that's fucked about being a celebrity. Yeah, or having living with one or having sex with one or a relationship or whatever we're doing here.
jokes.setup: Francine philosophically explains stalker psychology to Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry punctures the philosophical moment by noting the specific costs to Francine — 'living with one or having sex with one or a relationship or whatever we're doing here' — the trailing 'whatever we're doing here' revealing they can't even define their relationship
jokes.explanation: The trailing hedge — 'or whatever we're doing here' — is the key comedy beat. Larry deflects from his own celebrity neurosis to land on his relationship anxiety, which is simultaneously a character reveal and a good joke. The escalating list ('living with one, having sex with one, a relationship') is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What would it cost to have the bunker saddam hussein has?

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: He means that secure.

jokes.text: Oh, it's O.K. It's Tom Hanks. He always jogs at this time. Tom!
jokes.setup: Larry panics seeing someone run by outside
jokes.punchline: Francine casually identifies it as Tom Hanks jogging — as if this is a perfectly routine neighborhood occurrence — and cheerfully calls out to him
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Francine's absolute casual acceptance of Tom Hanks jogging past as a normal event. The 'He always jogs at this time' with the added 'Tom!' friendly wave is perfectly pitched celebrity-neighborhood absurdism. Shows the world of the show efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just can't believe I spent the money to move the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That was a wise decision, kiddo. Who wants to walk that far in the middle of the night to take a shit?

jokes.text: What would it cost to have the bunker Saddam Hussein has? He means that secure.
jokes.setup: Larry is consulting with a security company
jokes.punchline: Larry's security ideal is literally Saddam Hussein's bunker — the Security rep has to clarify this means Larry wants equivalent security, not the actual bunker
jokes.explanation: Larry's paranoia has escalated to identifying with Saddam Hussein as a security model, which is absurd but perfectly in character. The rep's deadpan clarification adds a layer. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Has he ever asked about my configuration?

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: Larry, would you like a brownie?

jokes.text: Security consultant clarifying: 'He means that secure' — after Saddam bunker comment
jokes.setup: Larry asks for Saddam Hussein's bunker
jokes.punchline: The consultant translates for his partner: 'he means that secure' — as if the request needs diplomatic clarification, which only highlights the absurdity further
jokes.explanation: A good button on the Saddam joke. The straight-faced professional translation from 'Saddam's bunker' to 'that secure' is the professional trying to stay on script while acknowledging the absurdity. Economy is high — five words that reframe everything.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: No. A fan sent them in for you and Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Why didn't you say something? Who knows what could be in these?

jokes.text: Why don't you add bars? I'll live like the Birdman of Alcatraz.
jokes.setup: The security consultant is proposing window filaments
jokes.punchline: Larry objects to window bars by invoking the Birdman of Alcatraz — a prisoner — as the extreme he's trying to avoid, while simultaneously making his house sound like a prison regardless
jokes.explanation: Decent character joke — Larry's objections to security measures are always framed in terms of how they'll make him look/feel. The Birdman reference works as a culturally specific self-deprecating image. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You want me to hire a taster? No. We don't need to hire a taster. Just have that weird intern do it.

jokes.text: Are you familiar with a book called Helter Skelter? Jack, the hard sell isn't really necessary.
jokes.setup: The security consultant is trying to convince Larry to install more security
jokes.punchline: The consultant name-drops Helter Skelter (the Manson family murders) as a sales tool; Larry's rep (Artie or Beverly) has to walk him back — the comedy is in the completely inappropriate but logically consistent hard sell
jokes.explanation: Callback to the John Lennon/Sharon Tate fear-mongering from the brochure — now in person. The consultant escalates from murder victims in a pamphlet to actually reciting Helter Skelter. Competent but the brochure joke set it up better.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: A few minutes. I waited for the right time.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, good choice.

jokes.text: Where did you get this blueprint of my house? It's on file at the assessor's office, readily available to any random kook out there.
jokes.setup: Larry is alarmed to see the security company has a blueprint of his house
jokes.punchline: The consultant's answer — it's publicly available to 'any random kook' — is meant to be reassuring but is the most alarming possible thing he could say
jokes.explanation: The 'readily available to any random kook out there' as a calming statement is beautifully constructed irony. The consultant is technically providing context but functionally making things worse. Strong structure — the punchline is in the exact wording of the explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A fucking puppet show? What are you do--

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Say hello to peace of mind.

jokes.text: I just can't believe I spent the money to move the bathroom. That was a wise decision, kiddo. Who wants to walk that far in the middle of the night to take a shit? That's what I was figuring.
jokes.setup: The house blueprint reveals the bathroom placement
jokes.punchline: Artie enthusiastically validates Larry's bathroom-moving decision on purely biological grounds — 'who wants to walk that far in the middle of the night to take a shit' — with zero embarrassment, as if this is wisdom to be shared
jokes.explanation: Artie's utterly pragmatic comfort with bathroom logistics as high wisdom is a lovely character moment. 'That's what I was figuring' from Larry confirms he takes this seriously. The mundane bathroom discussion in the middle of a security meeting is good tonal comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: This is the original handgun fired by jack lord on hawaii five-o. He gave it to me on my birthday.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You must be a big fan.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No. I've never seen it, but don't tell jack.

jokes.text: Is this the configuration Letterman has? Mr. Sanders, I'm sure you'll understand I can't comment on that, just as I would not tell Mr. Letterman about your configuration, if he asked me. I understand. Has he ever asked about my configuration?
jokes.setup: Larry asks if his security configuration matches Letterman's
jokes.punchline: After receiving a perfectly professional non-answer about confidentiality, Larry's follow-up — 'Has he ever asked about my configuration?' — reveals his real concern isn't security but whether Letterman thinks about him
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak. The security consultation is completely hijacked by Larry's competitive anxiety about Letterman. The security rep gives a textbook professional confidentiality answer; Larry's follow-up — 'Has he ever asked about my configuration?' — is one of the most character-perfect lines in the episode. It reframes the entire conversation: Larry doesn't want the best security, he wants Letterman to want his security. The character integration is exceptional — this joke could only exist in this show, with this character. Comparable to an 8.0+ anchor: specific, earned, character-defining, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Me, neither. Apparently, you just point and squeeze. That's what they tell me.
That's what who tells you?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Don't ask.

jokes.text: Larry, would you like a brownie? Thank you, Darlene. Phoebe? Oh, yeah. Coconut? Did your mom make these? No. A fan sent them in for you and Hank.
jokes.setup: Beverly/Darlene offers brownies during the serious security meeting
jokes.punchline: The revelation that the brownies were sent in by 'a fan' — during a stalker crisis, during a meeting about security — is the setup for the poisoning paranoia that follows
jokes.explanation: Well-timed misdirect. The casual brownie offer in the middle of a security consultation is funny in itself; the reveal that they're from a fan is the perfect dark punchline given the context. The moment is structured to maximize the comic irony.

dialogue.line: Aren't you the only saturday night live guy without some big movie deal?

jokes.text: You want me to hire a taster? No. We don't need to hire a taster. Just have that weird intern do it.
jokes.setup: Larry is worried the brownies might be poisoned
jokes.punchline: The solution isn't a professional taster — that would be excessive — just the 'weird intern,' who is disposable and already weird
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'professional taster' (too much) to 'just use the weird intern' (barely human) is a perfect showbiz-callousness joke. The casual 'weird intern' as the designated potential-poison tester reveals the Hollywood pecking order brilliantly. Quotable and dark.

dialogue.speaker: Phil Hartman
dialogue.line: Larry, I have a slumber party with my obsessed fans. We break out the sleeping bags. Order pizza, watch everything I've done on video, then spend hours talking about me.

jokes.text: Say hello to peace of mind. [produces gun] Is this loaded?
jokes.setup: Hank produces a handgun as his solution to Larry's stalker problem
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate first question — 'Is this loaded?' — is both a safety concern and an implicit terror that Hank Kingsley is handling a loaded weapon
jokes.explanation: The gun reveal as 'peace of mind' is good irony. Larry's immediate safety concern is a realistic response that functions as a character beat — he wants protection but clearly doesn't trust Hank with a weapon.

dialogue.speaker: Corbin Bernsen
dialogue.line: Yeah. I took 10 of my fans on a caribbean cruise.

dialogue.speaker: Corbin Bernsen
dialogue.line: You ever do that?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: This is the original handgun fired by Jack Lord on Hawaii Five-O. He gave it to me on my birthday. You must be a big fan. No. I've never seen it, but don't tell Jack.
jokes.setup: Hank reveals the gun is a TV prop from Jack Lord
jokes.punchline: Hank owns a treasured gift from Jack Lord but has never seen his show — he accepted the gift purely for the celebrity association, not any actual fandom
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Hank's relationship to celebrity — he values the currency of celebrity association over actual interest in the work. 'I've never seen it, but don't tell Jack' is a great line. High character integration because it's a very specific Hank pathology.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: What is your worst vacation?

dialogue.speaker: Fred
dialogue.line: Uh... I lost $250 in reno.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: Look at that. How?

dialogue.speaker: Fred
dialogue.line: Slots.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: Slots!

jokes.text: It's a 9-millimeter Beretta. Apparently, it's the most efficient handgun in the world. Me, neither. Apparently, you just point and squeeze. That's what they tell me. That's what who tells you? Don't ask.
jokes.setup: Hank is describing the gun's capabilities
jokes.punchline: Hank has no gun training himself and is passing along his knowledge from an unnamed, apparently dubious source ('Don't ask') — he's as unqualified to advise on this as possible
jokes.explanation: 'That's what who tells you? Don't ask.' is a perfectly Hank answer — he has obtained a potentially illegal or at least suspicious firearm from an unspecified source and is offering it to Larry with zero training. The 'apparently, you just point and squeeze' firearms instruction is darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's 'cause you're not on TV every night. You don't know what it feels like. You're not out there having tour buses go by your house with fucking psychos coming in to smell your clothes.

jokes.text: Artie confiscates the gun from Hank at the door. 'And Jack's people are putting in metal detectors at the studio entrances. So, Hank — hand it over. This? [pause] I'll hang on to this. Thank you. Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Artie arrives and mentions metal detectors being installed
jokes.punchline: Artie's smooth confiscation of the gun — which Hank apparently has on his person — followed by the tiny 'Sorry' from Hank is a perfect physical comedy beat
jokes.explanation: Artie's matter-of-fact gun appropriation is executed perfectly. The pause where Hank seems to genuinely think about whether to comply, followed by the sheepish 'Sorry,' is a great physical-comedy-through-dialogue moment. The callback payoff on the gun subplot lands efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What do you two assholes have to say now?

jokes.text: You loaded tonight? Just a little. That's what I thought.
jokes.setup: Phil Hartman asks Corbin Bernsen 'You loaded tonight?'
jokes.punchline: In context it means drunk; it echoes the gun conversation that just happened; and Bernsen's 'just a little' is a perfectly calibrated admission
jokes.explanation: The double meaning of 'loaded' (drunk/armed) works as an accidental callback given the preceding gun conversation. The deadpan 'that's what I thought' is a nice tag. The joke is mostly in the wordplay and the Hartman delivery implied.

dialogue.line: [Speaking spanish] Excuse me.

jokes.text: Yes, Phil. We got the old producers back. The show's getting really exciting. Tune in sometime. I will tune in. Aren't you the only Saturday Night Live guy without some big movie deal?
jokes.setup: Bernsen defends his show; Hartman says he'll tune in
jokes.punchline: Hartman returns the status attack — pointing out Hartman is the only SNL alum without a film career (accurate at the time) — turning it into a genuine celebrity trash-talk exchange
jokes.explanation: The counter-attack is perfectly targeted and historically accurate — Hartman did lack a major film career compared to contemporaries. The exchange functions as authentic celebrity pissing contest comedy. The 'Come on, come on — we're all in the same business, kidding, kidding' defusion is also a nice beat. High character integration since this is Hartman playing a version of himself.

dialogue.speaker: Police
dialogue.line: So he, basically, has no idea who I am.

dialogue.speaker: Police
dialogue.line: No, he doesn't.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah. I see.

jokes.text: Larry, I have a slumber party with my obsessed fans. We break out the sleeping bags. Order pizza, watch everything I've done on video, then spend hours talking about me. It's great.
jokes.setup: Larry is discussing how to manage obsessed fans; Phil says he neutralizes them
jokes.punchline: Phil's method is to have slumber parties — complete with pizza and video screenings of his own work — turning a potentially dangerous dynamic into a vanity-driven hang
jokes.explanation: Hartman's slumber party solution is a brilliant absurdist comedic image. The escalating details — sleeping bags, pizza, watching everything he's done on video, 'then spend hours talking about me' — each add to the absurdity. It works because the unstated implication is that Hartman enjoys this arrangement. The phrase 'spend hours talking about me' as a benefit rather than a warning sign is the key character comedy beat. Strong joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If you only had the electrical fence, all you'd have to do now is unplug it and hose it down.

jokes.text: In fact, one of them's with me right now. The guy in the green vest.
jokes.setup: Phil says he lets obsessed fans spend time with him
jokes.punchline: Phil casually reveals that one of his obsessed fans is literally present in the room right now — the fan Larry has been talking to as a normal person is actually an obsessive
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed reveal. The entire conversation about managing obsessed fans has been illustrated in real-time — Hartman has been coolly demonstrating his method while talking about it. The timing is excellent. Larry's reaction (going to greet the fan normally) and the 'I know you' beat make it even better. This recontextualizes the preceding conversation with great structural efficiency.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He had no idea who you were?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: None.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: My god, I'm sorry.

jokes.text: I took 10 of my fans on a Caribbean cruise. You ever do that? No.
jokes.setup: Phil Hartman has described his slumber party method; Corbin Bernsen tops it
jokes.punchline: Bernsen's casual mention of taking 10 fans on a Caribbean cruise as if it's a perfectly sensible celebrity fan management strategy
jokes.explanation: The escalation from slumber party to Caribbean cruise is well-structured. Larry's flat 'No' is perfect. The absurdity is that both Hartman and Bernsen have systematized their fan obsessions into elaborate hospitality arrangements while Larry can't manage one.

jokes.text: Who's the guy with the sunglasses? That's my manager, Mark Gervitz. Get him out of here. He scares me.
jokes.setup: Larry notices a man in sunglasses in the room
jokes.punchline: The man is just Bernsen's manager — but Larry's paranoia is now so heightened that a man in sunglasses registers as a threat requiring immediate removal
jokes.explanation: A good beat showing how Larry's paranoia has generalized from the stalker to everyone who looks vaguely threatening. 'He scares me' as a reason to remove someone from your own office is funny. Economical.

jokes.text: Larry asks who 'the guy with the sunglasses' is — it's his manager — Larry: 'Get him out of here. He scares me.'
jokes.setup: After the stalker discussion, Larry notices an unfamiliar person in the room
jokes.punchline: It's Corbin's manager — and Larry's immediate response is 'Get him out of here. He scares me.' The paranoia is now indiscriminate
jokes.explanation: Paranoia-escalation joke. Larry's stalker anxiety has now generalized to 'anyone with sunglasses inside.' The delivery and the specificity of 'He scares me' is perfectly Larry — immediate, personal, non-negotiable.

jokes.text: The pitch session collapses as Larry gets distracted by security — drill whirring, locksmith in the room, Larry can't focus
jokes.setup: Writers are trying to pitch monologue material while a locksmith drills in the background
jokes.punchline: The pitch session is completely undermined by paranoia infrastructure — 'He's throwing me off. He's putting in all the new locks. This is really important. Can't wait.' — the comedy of broken professional routine
jokes.explanation: Sustained cringe comedy as Larry's paranoid home-security project destroys his professional work environment. The 'can't wait' from the writer is dry and good. The scene as a whole works as workplace-dysfunction comedy.

jokes.text: Fred? Fred? Is it Fred? Yeah. What is your worst vacation? Uh... I lost $250 in Reno. How? Slots. [Chuckles] Slots!
jokes.setup: Larry is being convinced to try a segment where audience members share worst vacation stories
jokes.punchline: Fred's worst vacation — losing $250 at slots in Reno — is hilariously mundane as the concept's punchline, and Larry's 'Slots!' with a delighted chuckle is the reaction joke
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the anti-climax — the 'worst vacation' the concept is tested on is about as undramatic as possible. Larry's genuine delight at 'Slots!' is a good character beat — he's easily entertained by the mundane when he's not preoccupied. The 'Look at that' sets up the punchline nicely.

jokes.text: Writer suggests asking audience member Fred about his 'best vacation' — Larry corrects 'worst vacation' — Fred loses $250 in Reno on slots
jokes.setup: Writers are pitching a segment idea about asking audience members about their worst vacation
jokes.punchline: The test run is performed on Fred the locksmith who happens to be in the room — Fred's 'worst vacation' is losing $250 in Reno at slots — a completely mundane and anticlimactic answer to what was meant to prove a comedic concept
jokes.explanation: A layered joke: the writers test their segment concept on an unwilling test subject (the locksmith) and his completely ordinary answer ($250 in Reno, slots) perfectly illustrates why this is a bad idea for TV. Larry's 'Look at that. How? Slots' is beautiful deadpan — he's both impressed by the specificity and clearly disappointed by the material. The joke undermines the pitch while demonstrating the segment's premise.

jokes.text: What about the Hillary Clinton diary piece? The whole thing is in code. Actually, it's a music box.
jokes.setup: Writers are trying to pitch Larry during the security chaos
jokes.punchline: The Hillary Clinton diary is apparently a music box — the jump from 'it's in code' to 'actually, it's a music box' is absurdist and unexplained
jokes.explanation: The joke relies on chaos and unexplained absurdism. The 'music box' non-sequitur in response to 'it's in code' is funny primarily through bewilderment. It doesn't build to anything but captures the chaos of the writers' room trying to work around Larry's distraction.

jokes.text: Shouldn't it be Bill Clinton diary? He's the president, isn't he? I know. That's not this joke.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to engage with the Hillary Clinton diary piece during chaos
jokes.punchline: Larry's correction — 'isn't he the president?' — reveals he thinks a Hillary diary is less interesting than a Bill diary, while the writer's 'that's not this joke' implies they know something Larry doesn't about the joke's premise
jokes.explanation: A mild satirical beat about gender dynamics in political comedy — Larry defaulting to the male president as the more interesting subject. The 'that's not this joke' is a good defensive writer's line. Functional.

jokes.text: You think I'm overreacting to this security thing. That's 'cause you're not on TV every night. You don't know what it feels like. You're not out there having tour buses go by your house with fucking psychos coming in to smell your clothes.
jokes.setup: Hartman and Bernsen haven't said anything critical but Larry reads their silence as judgment
jokes.punchline: Larry's accusatory rant — particularly 'coming in to smell your clothes' — is the escalation that gives away exactly what happened in the office earlier, volunteering information that confirms his paranoia
jokes.explanation: The callback to the jacket-sniffing is both a comedy payoff and a character revelation — Larry is so wound up he can't stop himself from confessing the exact details of his humiliation to his guests. 'Coming in to smell your clothes' as the specific indignity he's defending against is very good. High character integration.

jokes.text: We didn't say anything. No, you're insinuating my concentration is fucked. If I'm not mistaken. So, Bill Clinton's diary? I can't think about that right now.
jokes.setup: Larry has just accused everyone of thinking he's overreacting
jokes.punchline: Larry instantly pivots to trying to work on the Bill Clinton bit — 'I can't think about that right now' — after explicitly stating he can't focus, he tries to prove he can by immediately failing to
jokes.explanation: The self-defeating pivot is a nice beat. Larry's insistence on proving he's functional immediately undermined by 'I can't think about that right now' is solid character comedy.

jokes.text: Larry, Francine just called. The security people caught somebody in your house. Is she O.K.? Just a little shaken. Everything's all right? She's fine. What do you two assholes have to say now?
jokes.setup: Larry has just been defending his paranoia to Hartman and Bernsen
jokes.punchline: A stalker has actually broken into his house — perfect vindication — and Larry's 'What do you two assholes have to say now?' to guests who never actually criticized him is the aggressive release
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the episode's central thread. Larry's paranoia is validated at the exact moment he was most aggressively defending it — and his triumphant 'what do you two assholes have to say now?' to guests who said nothing is perfectly in character. The timing is excellent sitcom craft. High character integration because Larry's vindication speech is an attack on people who weren't attacking him.

jokes.text: No, I don't live here. I just started seeing my ex-husband again, and I always end up staying over here. I don't know why. Consequently, I end up leaving for work from here, which is a pain in the ass because my apartment is right next to my job.
jokes.setup: The show cuts to Francine explaining her living situation — presumably a confessional or aside
jokes.punchline: Francine's resigned, self-aware admission about her dysfunctional relationship dynamic — she knows it makes no logistical sense but she keeps doing it — is the comedy
jokes.explanation: A confessional moment that functions as relationship character comedy. The complaint about the commute ('my apartment is right next to my job') as the practical downside of emotional dysfunction is a perfectly Larry Sanders Show touch — the personal becomes logistical. Good character-building joke.

jokes.text: I was a big fan of Jerry Lewis, uh, even before the telethon. You're probably thinking, how could I like somebody who was so broad? But the Nutty Professor — I don't know — that's neither here nor there.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to connect with the burglar/supposed stalker by establishing common ground as 'fans'
jokes.punchline: Larry's attempt at connection starts with defending Jerry Lewis — including a pre-emptive defense of Lewis's broadness — and then catching himself mid-tangent with 'that's neither here nor there'
jokes.explanation: Larry talking to a supposed stalker about Jerry Lewis as a form of human connection is a deeply character-specific comedy beat. The defensiveness about Lewis's broadness — unprompted, to a potentially dangerous intruder — is pure Larry. 'That's neither here nor there' as a self-correction in this context is beautifully absurd. Only this character in this show could generate this joke.

jokes.text: And if you ever want to talk to me or see me, instead of coming here, call Beverly at my office, and she'll arrange for you to spend a few minutes talking to me whenever I can squeeze it in.
jokes.setup: Larry is giving the 'stalker' his fan management speech based on Phil Hartman's advice
jokes.punchline: Larry has adopted Phil's fan-management strategy — including the casual 'whenever I can squeeze it in' — while speaking to someone he genuinely believes broke into his house to kill him
jokes.explanation: Larry has so completely internalized Hartman's approach that he's applying it in real-time to what he believes is a genuine stalker. The 'whenever I can squeeze it in' casual qualifier is perfect showbiz self-importance applied to a potentially lethal situation. Good callback structure.

jokes.text: Does he speak any English at all? None. He's from Guatemala. He's only been in the country about four weeks. So he basically has no idea who I am. No, he doesn't.
jokes.setup: Larry has given an elaborate 'I'm a human being too' speech to his stalker
jokes.punchline: The entire emotional connection speech was delivered to a random Guatemalan immigrant burgler who has no idea who Larry Sanders is — complete structural reversal of the episode's stalker premise
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke — an extended structural misdirect that recontextualizes everything. The entire episode has been about celebrity paranoia and the dangers of fame, and the punchline is that the 'stalker' is just a random hungry immigrant who has no idea who Larry Sanders is. The revelation that Larry's elaborate human-connection speech went to someone who speaks no English and doesn't know him is perfectly calibrated dark comedy. It earns its high score: it's original (the paranoid celebrity whose big validation is meaningless), structurally superb (the entire episode is the setup), deeply character-specific (Larry's entire identity is built on being known), and earned rather than cheap. Comparable in quality to the top anchor examples.

jokes.text: He's broken into several homes around here in the last few days. Random thievery. Probably needs money to bring his family over.
jokes.setup: Larry has just processed that the 'stalker' doesn't know who he is
jokes.punchline: The flatly delivered context — random burgler, family back home — makes Larry's entire paranoid episode seem even more pathetic. The word 'probably' is doing a lot of work
jokes.explanation: The follow-up to the big reveal. 'Probably needs money to bring his family over' is a darkly humanizing detail that makes Larry's ego-driven paranoia seem even more hollow. The deadpan delivery maximizes the contrast.

jokes.text: You know, I really feel like an idiot. You're not an idiot. Everybody gets paranoid nowadays. That's O.K. I don't think I was being paranoid.
jokes.setup: Larry has just gone through the humiliating revelation
jokes.punchline: Francine reassures him he wasn't being paranoid — just after he said he feels like an idiot — and he immediately rejects the comfort to defend his paranoia was actually justified
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'I feel like an idiot' to immediately rejecting the comfort to insist he wasn't actually paranoid is perfect Larry. He'd rather be right about his neurosis than be comforted. Beautifully character-specific.

jokes.text: Tour bus drives by after the anti-climactic resolution — Larry stiffens
jokes.setup: Larry and Francine are standing outside after the burglar has been taken away; Larry has just said he doesn't think he was being paranoid
jokes.punchline: A tour bus audibly passes. Larry goes quiet. We should really go in. Larry doesn't move.
jokes.explanation: A near-wordless callback that does enormous structural work. After everything — the fake stalker, the revealed burglar, the deflation of his paranoia — a tour bus drives by and Larry is right back where he started. The scene is essentially silent (implied by 'We should really go in') and Larry's inability to move is the joke. This is the episode's structural coda, not just a joke — but it functions as a brilliant comedic button. The economy of the moment (no one needs to say anything) is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: What happened? That obsessed fan broke into Larry's house. Oh, my god! If you only had the electrical fence, all you'd have to do now is unplug it and hose it down.
jokes.setup: Hank hears about the break-in and is outraged
jokes.punchline: Artie's response to the break-in is to regret the missed opportunity for lethal electric fence deployment — 'unplug it and hose it down' — delivered with total pragmatic calm
jokes.explanation: The callback to the electrical fence argument is devastating. 'All you'd have to do now is unplug it and hose it down' is one of the episode's best lines — Artie has mentally rehearsed the protocol for disposing of a dead intruder and delivers it with the calm efficiency of a man describing routine maintenance. The character integration is outstanding: only Artie could say this, only to Larry, only on this show. The contrast of 'unplug' (clinical) and 'hose it down' (visceral) is excellent word economy.

jokes.text: And, uh... He was a... You know, mixed-up guy who absolutely just, uh... Understood that we're both human beings. I don't think he'll be trouble anymore. Come on. Don't we have a show to do?
jokes.setup: Larry describes his interaction with the 'stalker' after the fact
jokes.punchline: Larry has reframed his humiliating interaction with a Guatemalan burglar who doesn't speak English as a successful human connection — and then pivots to showbiz pragmatism: 'Don't we have a show to do?'
jokes.explanation: Larry's self-serving narrative reconstruction — turning a humiliation into a success story — followed immediately by the showbiz 'Don't we have a show to do?' is perfect character comedy. The gap between what actually happened and how Larry tells it is enormous, and the pivot to professionalism is how he buries the humiliation. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Because it's fucking scary out there. I mean, if you have a demented fan, I have a demented fan. These people watch this show. They see me, half the time.
jokes.setup: Hank is expressing concern to Larry after the break-in
jokes.punchline: Hank's claim to equally threatening fan attention — 'they see me half the time' — is the punchline; the sidekick is visible in half the shots and therefore thinks he has half the stalker risk
jokes.explanation: 'They see me half the time' as a claim to equivalent celebrity stalker risk is a perfect Hank line — his status calculation is done entirely in terms of screen time percentages. The character integration is very high because this is exactly how Hank would think about fame. Quotable and specific.

jokes.text: I have a gun, but Artie won't let me bring my gun anymore.
jokes.setup: Hank is discussing his own security concerns
jokes.punchline: Hank has already been disarmed by Artie earlier in the episode — a fact he accepts with resigned sadness, as if this is an ongoing situation rather than a one-time confiscation
jokes.explanation: The 'Artie won't let me bring my gun anymore' implies this is an established pattern, not just a one-time incident. Hank's resigned acceptance of being disarmed as a regular workplace policy is very funny. The callback enriches the earlier joke and adds to Hank's character portrait.

jokes.text: It was a completely random burglar. The guy had no fucking idea who I was. No clue whatsoever. He had no idea who you were? None. My god, I'm sorry.
jokes.setup: Larry tells Hank the truth about the 'stalker'
jokes.punchline: Hank's reaction — 'My god, I'm sorry' — as if the true tragedy is that the burglar didn't know who Larry was, not the burglary itself
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's emotional kicker. Hank's 'My god, I'm sorry' as condolence for the burglar's ignorance — not for the break-in — crystallizes everything the show is saying about celebrity and identity. Both Larry and Hank agree that being unknown is worse than being robbed. The economy is perfect. The character integration is superb — this reaction is pure Hank but it also reflects Larry's own feelings. One of the episode's strongest beats.

jokes.text: Larry... Did you tell some Javier he could see you tomorrow? Yeah. Would you get Corbin Bernsen on the phone?
jokes.setup: Larry has just told Hank the burglar had no idea who he was
jokes.punchline: Larry has — apparently — arranged for Javier the burglar to come back and see him (applying Phil Hartman's fan management advice to a literal burglar), and his follow-up is to call Corbin Bernsen — presumably to get the Caribbean cruise idea
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and one of its best. Larry has invited the random burglar back for a meeting, and his call to Corbin Bernsen implies he's planning to take the burglar on a Caribbean cruise — having fully internalized the celebrity fan-management strategies and applied them to someone who burgled his home and has no idea who he is. The structural callback to every fan-management conversation in the episode lands perfectly. Only Larry Sanders could end an episode this way: ego-driven, self-defeating, and completely committed. The character integration score is maximum — this is the entire show distilled into a closing beat.

tmdb_overview: Larry gets a little paranoid when he learns he's being stalked by an obsessed fan.
